title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 9
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Substance That Made Seeing Possible
passages.text:
A. Glass is usually catalogued among decorative materials, and its ornamental history is long and well documented. The more consequential history is instrumental. Two devices built from shaped glass — the telescope and the microscope — opened ranges of observation that no amount of unaided attention could reach, and the sciences that followed were not refinements of existing knowledge but investigations of things nobody had known existed.

B. That this happened where it did is partly a matter of chemistry rather than genius. Producing glass clear enough to shape into a lens requires raw materials low in iron, which tints the result green, and furnaces capable of sustained high temperature. Regions with suitable sand and established furnace traditions developed optical glass; regions without them produced glass that was serviceable for vessels and useless for instruments. Skill was widely distributed; the inputs were not.

C. The lens preceded the theory that explained it by a long interval, which is the usual order and not the exception. Spectacles were in use for centuries before anyone described refraction adequately, and early telescopes were assembled by craftsmen combining lenses empirically. Understanding followed the artefact and then improved it — a sequence in which practice generates the phenomenon that theory subsequently accounts for, and which the popular account of science generally reverses.

D. The instrument's authority was not immediate and the resistance was reasonable. An observer reporting features on a distant body was asking others to trust a device that demonstrably produced distortions, coloured fringes and, in poorly made examples, entirely spurious detail. The question of whether the instrument showed what was there or what it introduced was a serious one, and it was settled not by argument but by convergence: independent observers with independently made instruments reporting the same features.

E. Improvements that mattered most were unglamorous corrections of defects. Different colours refract by different amounts, so a simple lens focuses them at different points and surrounds every image with a fringe. Combining glasses of differing composition so that the dispersion of one offsets the other largely removed this, and the resulting instruments were not more powerful in any simple sense — they were merely accurate, which turned out to be the property that mattered.

F. The pattern recurs in every subsequent extension of observation. Detectors sensitive to radiation the eye cannot register, and instruments recording at scales the hand cannot manipulate, have each raised the same question the early telescope raised, and have each been settled the same way: by agreement between instruments built on different principles. The lesson is not that instruments are trustworthy but that convergence between independent ones is, which is a weaker claim and the only one the history supports.

passages.title: The Archive in the Ice
passages.text:
Snow falling on a polar ice sheet does not melt. It is buried by later snow, compressed, and preserved, and because each year's fall is distinguishable from the next, a vertical core drilled through the sheet is a sequence in time — the deepest ice being the oldest. The longest cores recovered reach back hundreds of thousands of years, and the record they hold is unusually direct.

What makes the record unusual is that the ice contains the atmosphere itself. As snow compacts, air is trapped in bubbles, and that air is a physical sample of what the atmosphere contained when the bubble sealed. Most reconstructions of past climate are indirect — inferred from tree rings, sediments or isotope ratios that respond to conditions — whereas the gas in an ice core is not a proxy for past air. It is past air.

Temperature must still be inferred, and the method rests on a physical regularity rather than an assumption. Water molecules containing heavier oxygen and hydrogen isotopes evaporate slightly less readily and condense slightly more readily, so the isotopic composition of precipitation varies with the temperature at which it formed. Calibrating that relationship against modern measurements yields a temperature history, with uncertainties that are real, quantified and considerably smaller than the variations being measured.

Dating a core is where most of the difficulty lies. Annual layers can be counted directly in the upper sections, as one counts tree rings, but layers thin under the weight above and eventually become indistinguishable. Below that point, dating depends on flow models, on chemical markers from volcanic eruptions of known date, and on matching features between cores from different sites. Uncertainty therefore grows with depth, and comparisons between records are stated with that uncertainty attached — a practice that outside readers sometimes mistake for weakness in the underlying data.

One structural feature of the record has been persistently misused. Gas diffuses within the porous upper layer before the bubbles close, so the air in a bubble is younger than the ice enclosing it, by an interval that varies with accumulation rate and must be modelled. This offset is well characterised, and it has been repeatedly presented by non-specialists as an unacknowledged flaw — a claim that survives only if one does not read the papers, which discuss it at length because it is the field's own long-standing problem.

What the cores established was not that climate changes, which was already known, but how fast it can. Records show transitions of substantial magnitude occurring within decades rather than millennia, which was not expected and which changed the questions being asked. A system that can move quickly is a different object from one that moves gradually, and much subsequent work has been an attempt to identify what mechanism permits the speed the ice recorded.

passages.title: Why Corrections Fail
passages.text:
A false claim, once circulated, is not removed by publishing an accurate one. This is among the more robust findings in the study of belief, and it is uncomfortable because the obvious remedy — supply the correct information — is the one the evidence says works least well.

Part of the explanation is mechanical rather than motivational. Repetition increases the sense that a statement is familiar, and familiarity is used as a rough proxy for truth. A correction that restates the false claim in order to deny it repeats it, and the denial is more easily forgotten than the claim. Corrections phrased around the accurate fact, without restating the falsehood, perform measurably better — a finding with immediate practical use that has been slow to reach the organisations issuing corrections.

A second element concerns explanatory coherence. People do not hold beliefs as isolated items but as parts of accounts that make events intelligible. Removing a claim from such an account leaves a gap, and a gap is uncomfortable in a way that a wrong answer is not. Corrections that supply an alternative explanation — not merely stating that the claim is false but saying what did happen — are substantially more effective, because they replace rather than delete.

The role of identity has been overstated in popular accounts and is real in a narrower form. On claims connected to group membership, people do process evidence differently, and correction can occasionally strengthen the original belief. But this backfire effect has proved much harder to reproduce than early reports suggested, and most corrections on most topics reduce belief in the false claim somewhat, including among those predisposed to accept it. The honest summary is that corrections usually work partially, rarely work completely, and occasionally fail — which is less dramatic than the version usually cited.

Timing is the variable with the largest measured effect and the least attention. Warning someone that they are about to encounter a misleading claim, and briefly explaining the technique being used, reduces its subsequent impact considerably more than correcting it afterwards. This asymmetry between prevention and repair is consistent across studies and points toward interventions that most institutions are poorly arranged to deliver, since it requires acting before a claim is prominent rather than after.

The uncomfortable implication concerns effort. Producing an accurate account is slow and producing a false one is not, so the two are not in symmetrical competition, and a system that responds only after publication is structurally behind. The evidence does not support the conclusion that correction is pointless. It supports the narrower and more awkward conclusion that correction is the least efficient of the available responses, and the one on which nearly all institutional effort is currently spent.
